articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related Entities, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations, Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 21, 2026. Concurrently, OFAC removed certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea.

In addition to the designations and removals, OFAC issued new general licenses pertaining to Iran and Russia. The agency also published amended Frequently Asked Questions to provide further guidance on these actions.
These measures reflect ongoing adjustments to U.S. sanctions programs, targeting illicit activities while providing humanitarian and other authorized avenues for engagement.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements PAIPA Designations and Issues Associated General Licenses
body: On October 19, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA). These designations aim to counter threats to American intellectual property.

In conjunction with these new designations, OFAC also issued associated general licenses. These licenses are intended to mitigate unintended consequences and ensure that legitimate activities can continue.
The PAIPA designations underscore the U.S. government's commitment to safeguarding intellectual property rights globally and deterring theft and misappropriation.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Venezuela-related General License on October 16, 2026. This amendment modifies existing authorizations concerning transactions involving Venezuela.

Alongside the amended general license, OFAC also published an updated Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). This FAQ provides clarification and guidance on the scope and application of the revised authorization.
These adjustments are part of OFAC's ongoing efforts to fine-tune sanctions programs in response to evolving circumstances and policy objectives.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related and Cuba Entities, Issues New and Amended General Licenses
body: On October 15, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting entities related to Iran and Cuba. These actions aim to pressure the regimes in both countries.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued new and amended general licenses, along with updated Frequently Asked Questions. These documents provide guidance on authorized transactions and activities.
The designations reflect the U.S. government's continued focus on countering activities deemed destabilizing or repressive by the Iranian and Cuban governments.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation on October 14, 2026. This action indicates a recalibration of sanctions pressure on certain Venezuelan entities.

Designation removals can occur for various reasons, including a change in behavior by the designated party, a shift in U.S. policy, or a determination that the designation no longer serves its intended purpose.
This specific removal will likely impact the operational landscape for entities involved in transactions with Venezuela, potentially easing some restrictions.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: On October 13, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. These actions aim to disrupt illicit networks globally.
These designations fall under OFAC's broader efforts to combat international drug trafficking and terrorist financing, which pose significant threats to U.S. national security and foreign policy.
The Treasury Department continues to leverage its sanctions authorities to isolate and financially disrupt those who engage in these dangerous activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates International Criminal Court Officials, Issues General Licenses, Removes Burma Designation
body: On October 9, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations related to the International Criminal Court (ICC). This action was accompanied by the issuance of new general licenses.

In a separate but concurrent action, OFAC also announced the removal of a Burma-related designation. This removal signifies a change in the U.S. government's assessment of the designated entity or the broader situation in Burma.
These diverse actions highlight OFAC's dynamic approach to sanctions, responding to various geopolitical developments and policy priorities.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a new Russia-related General License on October 9, 2026. This license authorizes certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under existing sanctions programs.

General licenses are frequently used by OFAC to carve out specific activities or categories of transactions from broader sanctions, often to facilitate humanitarian aid, certain financial operations, or other policy-driven exceptions.
This new general license provides clarity and legal authorization for specific engagements involving Russia, reflecting ongoing adjustments to the sanctions regime.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related Entities, Issues New Iran-Related and Amended Russia-Related General Licenses
body: On October 8, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting entities involved with Iran. These actions are part of the ongoing pressure campaign against the Iranian regime.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued a new Iran-related General License and an amended Russia-related General License. These licenses aim to provide specific authorizations for certain transactions.
The combination of new designations and updated general licenses reflects OFAC's continuous efforts to implement and refine its sanctions programs to achieve foreign policy objectives.

articles.headline: Bank of America Fined $11,662,930 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Bank of America, N.A., resulting in a civil monetary penalty of $11,662,930. This penalty addresses apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs, including those related to Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

This OFAC penalty is part of a broader enforcement action against Bank of America, which also includes a $1.2 billion penalty from the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) and a $750 million civil money penalty from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) for Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and anti-money laundering (AML) deficiencies.

The bank admitted to willful violations of the BSA and failures in its AML program, including inadequate internal controls and a proprietary transaction monitoring system that resulted in missed and delayed detection of over $5 billion in suspicious activity.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Settles with OFAC for $175,015
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, resulting in a civil monetary penalty of $175,015. The details of the violations leading to this settlement were not immediately specified in the public announcement.

OFAC enforcement actions typically involve violations of U.S. sanctions programs, which can include engaging in prohibited transactions, dealing with sanctioned entities, or failing to implement adequate compliance controls.
This settlement underscores OFAC's continued vigilance in enforcing sanctions regulations across various industries and against entities globally.

articles.headline: US Inflation Accelerates to 3.7% in September, Driven by Energy Prices
body: The U.S. annual inflation rate accelerated to 3.7% in September 2026, up from 3.4% in August, exceeding market expectations of 3.6%. This increase was primarily driven by higher energy prices, with gasoline rising 34.2% year-over-year and fuel oil prices increasing 74.2%.

On a monthly basis, the Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 0.6% in September, marking its largest gain in five months, with gasoline accounting for over half of this increase. Inflation also accelerated for shelter, while food price inflation slowed.

The inflation data comes just days before the Federal Reserve's interest rate decision, with economists divided on whether the Fed will raise rates again or hold them steady. The data also puts pressure on Republicans ahead of the midterm elections.
articles.source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics / Al Jazeera

articles.headline: Lula Wins Historic Fourth Term as Brazilian President, Bolsonaro Refuses to Concede
body: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has secured a historic fourth term as Brazil's president, defeating far-right opponent Flávio Bolsonaro in a dramatic election fightback. With 100% of votes counted, the 80-year-old leftist received 51.79% of the vote, a margin of 4.4 million votes over Bolsonaro's 48.21%.

Bolsonaro, however, has refused to concede defeat and has asked for the results to be annulled. Lula's victory marks a significant comeback, as he narrowly lost the first round of the election in early October.

International leaders, including Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and Paraguayan President Santiago Peña, have congratulated Lula on his victory, while confirmation of his win was met with anger in Brasília, where Bolsonaro is under house arrest.

articles.headline: UN Human Rights Chief Condemns Escalation of Drone Strikes in Sudan, 306 Killed
body: UN human rights chief Volker Türk has strongly condemned an escalation in drone strikes across Sudan this month, which have resulted in the deaths of at least 306 people and injured hundreds more in the first three weeks of October alone.

The World Food Programme also reported an airstrike on a United Nations truck in South Kordofan, Sudan, which killed the driver. These incidents highlight the severe impact of the ongoing conflict on civilians and humanitarian efforts.
The escalating violence underscores the urgent need for a cessation of hostilities and protection of civilians in Sudan, as the humanitarian crisis continues to worsen.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions for October 2026, Including Penalties Against American Express and Bank of America
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released its enforcement actions for October 2026, including significant penalties against American Express National Bank and Bank of America, National Association.

American Express National Bank was issued a Cease and Desist Order and a $350 million civil money penalty for deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and customer due diligence and customer identification program violations.

Bank of America, National Association, also received a civil money penalty of $750 million for deficiencies in its BSA compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and sending wires with inaccurate transmittor name information. The OCC also issued Orders of Prohibition against two institution-affiliated parties for embezzlement.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

articles.headline: OCC Finalizes GENIUS Act Rule on Stablecoin Yield, Retains Evasion Scrutiny
body: On October 21, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced its final GENIUS Act rule, effective January 18, 2027. The rule addresses the prohibition on payment of interest or yield solely in connection with holding, using, or retaining a payment stablecoin.

The OCC removed a proposed rebuttable presumption concerning stablecoin rewards but affirmed its authority to address evasion of the yield prohibition. The agency will apply the statute to each arrangement based on all relevant facts and circumstances, rather than providing broad safe harbors.

The final rule also covers permitted and foreign payment stablecoin issuers under OCC jurisdiction and certain custody activities. Bank Secrecy Act, anti-money laundering, and sanctions provisions will be addressed in a separate rulemaking coordinated with the Treasury Department.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency / DeFi Prime

body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) today announced a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A. (bank), for violations of the Bank Secrecy Act and its implementing regulations, including 12 CFR 21.21 and 12 CFR 21.11. This amount is the largest in OCC history.

articles.headline: FinCEN Assesses $1.2 Billion Penalty Against Bank of America for BSA/AML Violations
body: The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) announced a $1.2 billion civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A., for willful failures to implement and maintain certain anti-money laundering (AML) program requirements, conduct due diligence on foreign financial institution correspondent accounts, and file accurate and timely suspicious activity reports (SARs).

The consent order found that the bank's critical deficiencies and gaps in its proprietary transaction monitoring system resulted in missed and delayed detection and reporting of over $5 billion of suspicious activity, with approximately $1 billion implicating national security-related and other priority illicit finance risks, including Chinese Money Laundering Networks and potential trade-based money laundering.

FinCEN credited the $750 million civil money penalty assessed concurrently by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) against Bank of America for its deficient BSA/AML compliance program, meaning the bank will pay $450 million directly to FinCEN.

articles.headline: BIS Clarifies License Requirements for Advanced Computing Items to Entities Headquartered in Country Group D:5 and Macau
body: The Department of Commerce, Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), has issued guidance clarifying that a license is required to export advanced computing items to entities headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau, or with an ultimate parent company headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. This requirement applies even if the entities themselves are located outside these regions.

This guidance aims to prevent circumvention of export controls on advanced computing items, which are critical for national security. Country Group D:5 includes countries of concern for national security reasons.
The clarification reinforces BIS's commitment to controlling the export of sensitive technologies to prevent their use in ways that undermine U.S. security interests.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
